    Breaking: The Party Shaping Spain’s Election Isn’t Even on the Ballot

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2140 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that catalonia’s independence movement is moving to the right, and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez might pay the price in snap parliamentary elections on Nov.
    • Sánchez called elections after failing to get emergency legislation aimed at tackling Spain’s housing crisis through parliament in October.
    • It has been revealed that catalonia’s independence movement is moving to the right, and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez might pay the price in snap parliamentary elections on Nov.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Get audio access with any FP subscription.

    Industry observers note that catalonia’s independence movement is moving to the right, and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez might pay the price in snap parliamentary elections on Nov. 29. Junts per Catalunya, the separatist party that supported Sánchez to form a minority government in 2023, turned against him last year to fend off a fresh far-right rival—ultimately forcing the early vote.

    Sánchez called elections after failing to get emergency legislation aimed at tackling Spain’s housing crisis through parliament in October. The conservative People’s Party (PP), the far-right Vox party, and the center-right Junts all voted against the package.

    It has been revealed that catalonia’s independence movement is moving to the right, and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez might pay the price in snap parliamentary elections on Nov. 29. Junts per Catalunya, the separatist party that supported Sánchez to form a minority government in 2023, turned against him last year to fend off a newly introduced far-right rival—ultimately forcing the early vote.

    Sánchez called elections after failing to get emergency legislation aimed at tackling Spain’s housing crisis through parliament in October. The conservative People’s Party (PP), the far-right Vox party, and the center-right Junts all voted against the package.

    It was the latest example of Junts going against the minority government’s initiatives. When party head Carles Puigdemont announced that Junts would revoke its backing and move into the opposition last year, he blamed Sánchez’s Socialist Workers’ Party for broken promises. But the pro-independence party is also facing a growing threat at home in Catalonia.

    According to recent reports, that threat is Aliança Catalana—a far-right, separatist party led by Sílvia Orriols, the mayor of the small town of Ripoll. Orriols founded Aliança in 2020 after breaking with another separatist party; its platform combines a demand for Catalan independence with hard-line hostility toward immigration and Islam. She pushed for a tougher approach to immigration after the 2017 Barcelona attacks, carried out by a terror cell based in Ripoll.

    In a recent development, unlike Junts, Aliança has elected not to stand in the Nov. 29 national elections, refusing to take part based on its Catalonian separatism. “We are not thinking about influencing Madrid, and that’s part of the foundation of Aliança,” remarked the party’s press chief, Eduard Berraondo.

    Polling right now points to a right-wing majority. The PP leads with 31.2 percent of the vote, with the Socialists at 29.3 percent, and Vox at 18 percent as of Nov. 24, according to newspaper Ara’s polling average. Together, the PP and Vox are projected to win around 190 seats, above the 176 needed for a majority in the 350-seat Congress of Deputies. Only the state-run Center for Sociological Studies pollster, which critics say favors the government, puts the Socialists ahead.

    So, although Aliança isn’t on the ballot, its rapid rise is reshaping Spanish politics.

    It has been revealed that the party’s hard line on immigration and Islam has pushed Junts to the right, making the party ever less likely to partner with the Socialists. Aliança’s voters could help decide where Catalonia’s right-wing vote goes: back to Junts, across to Vox, or nowhere at all. Finally, the party’s growing popularity suggests a deeper shift among Catalan independence supporters, away from progressivism and toward a more exclusionary view of who counts as Catalan.

    Industry observers note that aliança has risen rapidly in Catalonia. The far-right party won just two of 135 seats in the Catalan parliamentary elections in 2024, but the latest survey from the Catalan government’s polling agency, the Centre d’Estudis d’Opinió (CEO), projects that the party would capture between 23 and 25 seats if regional elections were held now. Junts, which holds 35 seats, would fall to between 18 and 20.

    Catalonia’s next regional elections must be held by late June 2028. Almost 1 in 5 people who voted for Junts in 2024 now say they would back Aliança—but a majority of those wavering respondents still ranked Junts as their second choice.

    Aliança’s message lands with voters anxious about rapid population growth, crime, and stretched public services. Around 18 percent of its supporters say they would vote for Vox on Nov. 29, according to the CEO. This matters in Madrid, where each seat that Junts loses weakens the leverage that once made it a kingmaker.

    According to recent reports, junts is responding to Aliança’s rise by shifting to the right. The party has demanded that Madrid hand Catalonia control over immigration, backed bans on the burqa and niqab in public spaces, and pushed for tougher rules on repeat criminal offenders. The party has also proposed making immigrants wait 10 years after registering as residents before they can apply for subsidized housing, more than three times the current maximum.

    Catalonia elects 48 members of Spain’s national parliament; Junts holds seven of those seats. In return for the party’s support after the 2023 election, the Socialists pushed through an amnesty law covering those involved in the 2017 Catalan independence push, including Puigdemont, who at the time served as Catalonia’s president and fled to Belgium to avoid arrest. The Supreme Court lifted his arrest warrant in October, clearing the way for his return.

    Recent findings suggest that junts has ruled out backing either Sánchez or the PP’s party leader for prime minister, though it has left the door open to supporting a different Socialist candidate. Competing with Aliança for allegiance in Catalonia, it has little room to prop up a left-wing government. With a PP-Vox majority, that might not matter. But if the right-wing vote falls short, Spain’s government could once again hang on a handful of Catalan votes.

    The CEO expects Junts to win just four or five parliamentary seats in the snap elections, while Vox could more than double its share of Catalonia’s seats—from two seats to five or six. Some of those votes might come from Aliança supporters.

    “From Nov. 29, a dual voter will emerge: someone who votes Aliança in municipal and Catalan elections, and Vox in Spanish ones,” said Xavier Torrens, a professor of political science at the University of Barcelona.

    Vox and Aliança are opposed when it comes to the question of Catalonia’s independence, but on immigration, they speak the same language.

    “Many people vote Vox because they reject immigration, feel unsafe, or believe immigrants take a large share of public benefits. Aliança notes the same,” said Xavier Rius, a Catalan journalist and the author of a book on Aliança.

    Berraondo rejected a direct comparison between his party and Vox, insisting that their positions overlap only on immigration and law and order and that Aliança does not share Vox’s opposition to abortion and gay rights.

    Still, Aliança might see a PP-Vox victory as good news for its future. “Imagine you think that if the PP and Vox win the elections in November, they could start the dirty job of changing the immigration rules,” Berraondo said. “Then you can take advantage of it if you are in government in Catalonia in 2028.”.

    Recent findings suggest that this political convergence would once have been unthinkable. The Catalan independence movement defined itself against the Spanish nationalism that Vox represents and long prided itself on being progressive, inclusive, and pro-European. Center-right parties joined the independence push in the 2010s, but Aliança is the first far-right separatist party to gain traction in Catalonia.

    In a recent development, so, how did a far-right party emerge from the movement, and why now? Part of the answer lies in 2017. That October, Catalonia’s pro-independence government held a referendum that Spain’s Constitutional Court had declared illegal. Puigdemont signed a declaration of independence and then days later confirmed that he asked parliament to suspended it. Weeks later, Madrid suspended Catalonia’s autonomy, and the movement’s leaders were jailed or fled abroad.

    For many Junts supporters, the promise that independence was within reach proved hollow. Puigdemont’s about-face and rush to negotiate with Madrid seemed to reveal that the party prioritized its political leverage over independence—a perception later reinforced when Junts backed Sanchez’s government and demanded amnesty for its leaders rather than any move toward independence.

    Orriols, the Aliança leader, has built her appeal on that sense of betrayal, casting the referendum moment as a deception and Puigdemont as a leader who lost his nerve. Voters who have switched allegiance from Junts to Aliança are, on average, around 56 years old, with nearly 89 percent supporting independence, according to the CEO. Their top concerns are immigration and insecurity. These are disappointed separatists—not newcomers to the cause.

    Industry observers note that “Part of Junts’s electorate realized that the whole narrative about independence was just fluff, that they weren’t serious about it,” said Massimo Maoret, a professor at IESE Business School in Barcelona and a longtime observer of Catalan politics. Aliança, he added, has tapped into that feeling “together with anti-immigrant, and especially anti-Islamic, sentiment.”.

    Further, as the cost of living rises, the concerns over affordable housing that brought down Sánchez’s government have also boosted the far-right party. Aliança “is winning an anti-system, anti-establishment vote, driven by people being fed up with the rising cost of living, the high cost of housing, and the poor functioning of public services such as rail transport,” Torrens mentioned.

    Aliança has drawn a connection between those problems and immigration, from pushing a debate over who counts as Catalan. For decades, the independence movement embraced a slogan popularized by Jordi Pujol, a former Catalan president: “Anyone who lives and works in Catalonia is Catalan.”.

    Aliança takes a different line. “Aliança considers that only some of Catalonia’s inhabitants are Catalan, while the rest are immigrants settled in Catalonia but not Catalan,” Torrens said. Orriols has said that Muslims could not be Catalan because “they don’t integrate with the country’s culture and values.”.

    Vox could unseat Pedro Sánchez in snap elections. How do you beat such an unusual party?

    Why Spain’s Sánchez has succeeded while Britain’s Starmer floundered.

    Sources indicate that the question is the extent to which Aliança is shaping the independence movement. Junts has already shifted toward some of Aliança’s positions on immigration—but Jordi Turull, Junts’s secretary-general, has warned that the far right “will do nothing but take us further from our goal of a prosperous and complete Catalan republic.”.

    Sources indicate that josep Vila, the president of the Catalan National Assembly, a grassroots pro-independence organization, declined to say whether Aliança belonged to the movement. The group was “not concerned by the diversity of political options,” Vila wrote in an email, as long as they shared a strategy for independence.

    In a recent development, meanwhile, Aliança’s base is broadening beyond the independence movement. According to the CEO, only 53 percent of its supporters now back independence, down from 62 percent late last year. Taken together, the data suggest a shift in priorities. For disillusioned separatists and newcomers alike, concerns about immigration, security, and the cost of living increasingly outweigh the question of independence.

    It has been revealed that in some ways, Catalonia seems to be following a familiar European script of an emergent far right—this time from within a separatist movement. Torrens makes a distinction between national-populist parties that took decades to break through, such as France’s National Rally, and those that do so within a few years, such as Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s Brothers of Italy, Portugal’s Chega, and Vox itself.

    According to recent reports, aliança, he said, is on the fast track. The party’s first test comes in this week’s snap elections, when its supporters could shape the outcome. The bigger tests come later: municipal elections in May 2027 and the regional election by 2028. For now, Aliança seems to have shifted the Catalan independence movement’s center of gravity, as a movement that prided itself on building a Catalonia for all has absorbed an us-versus-them view of who belongs.

    The Nov. 29 vote will offer the first signs of how far that shift reaches beyond Catalonia. If Junts loses seats in Madrid, and especially if the PP and Vox win a majority on their own, then Catalan separatists could lose their leverage over Spain’s government for the first time in years. The irony is that some of Aliança’s own supporters might help sweep the nationalists in.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that fox News legal editor Kerri Urbahn analyzes President Trump's new executive orders targeting birth tourism and birthright citizenship, plus the legal battle with the ACLU and a Texas hospital settlement. Urbahn discusses the constitutional battles ahead.

    A DC federal judge, previously dubbed by President Donald Trump as an "anti- Trump Hater," blocked Trump's second attempt to restrict birthright citizenship in a Wednesday ruling.

    U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper, who was recently in Trump's crosshairs after ruling against efforts to shut down the Kennedy Center for renovations and add Trump's name to the cultural institution, issued a 67-page ruling striking down an August executive order that barred U.S. -born children whose parents are suspected terrorists or gang members, or children born through surrogacy to foreign parents, from citizenship eligibility.

    Cooper's ruling comes months after the Supreme Court struck down Trump's initial executive order, signed on his first day back in office. The order attempted to deny birthright citizenship to U.S.-born children whose mothers were in the country illegally or temporarily and whose fathers were neither U.S. citizens nor green card holders.

    WHITE HOUSE RIPS ‘ACTIVIST’ BIDEN JUDGE WHO UPENDED TRUMP BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP ORDER.

    According to recent reports, demonstrators hold up an anti-Trump sign outside the U.S. Supreme Court in Washington, DC, on June 27, 2025, after the justices curbed nationwide injunctions in a case stemming from President Donald Trump's initial bid to end birthright citizenship. (ALEX WROBLEWSKI/AFP via Getty Images).

    "As the Supreme Court has made clear, however, the President cannot carve out new exceptions to birthright citizenship for children born within the United States and subject to its laws," Cooper ruled.

    It has been revealed that trump's second executive order was already partially blocked on Sept. 2 by U.S. District Judge Deborah Boardman in Maryland, whose injunction protected U.S.-born children of mothers who were in the country illegally or temporarily and whose fathers were neither U.S. citizens nor lawful permanent residents.

    Cooper's ruling expanded protections beyond that class to include additional children born to certain foreign government and international organization employees, parents deemed "alien enemies" by the administration and foreign parents who used commercial surrogacy services in the U.S.

    "The merits in this case are clear-cut. The Supreme Court has twice confirmed that all children born in this country are U.S. citizens, save only for the small handful who are not subject to U.S. law," Cooper wrote.

    In addition to the Supreme Court's June ruling in Trump v. Barbara, Cooper referred to the high court's ruling in United States v. Wong Kim Ark, which determined that a man born to Chinese immigrants was a protected U.S. citizen under the 14th Amendment.

    SEN ERIC SCHMITT SEEKS TO END BIRTH TOURISM, REVOKE CITIZENSHIP FOR BABIES OF FOREIGN DIPLOMATS.

    President Donald Trump speaks during a news conference in the James S. Brady Briefing Room at the White House in Washington, DC, on June 27, 2025, following a U.S. Supreme Court ruling on nationwide injunctions in litigation over his first birthright citizenship executive order. (Mehmet Eser/Middle East Images via AFP).

    Cooper noted that Wong Kim Ark established narrow exceptions to birthright citizenship, including for children of foreign diplomats, children born aboard foreign public ships and children of enemy forces occupying American territory.

    "While the Fourteenth Amendment may theoretically permit new exceptions beyond those listed in Wong Kim Ark, Congress has not authorized any such exceptions," Cooper wrote.

    It has been revealed that cooper argued that membership in a terrorist organization alone does not satisfy the historical exception to birthright citizenship for children of enemy forces occupying U.S. territory. He criticized the Trump administration's contention that foreign invaders could occupy American territory without actually holding it as an "outside-the-box understanding" of what constitutes an occupation.

    "To recap, a parent’s purported status as an alien enemy, standing alone, cannot strip a U.S.-born child of his right to birthright citizenship," Cooper wrote. "The alien-enemy exception, properly understood, applies only to children born to hostile enemy forces in temporarily occupied U.S. territory.".

    Industry observers note that cooper also rejected Trump's attempt to deny birthright citizenship to children born through commercial surrogacy arrangements involving foreign parents, finding that the circumstances of their birth do not exempt them from U.S. jurisdiction.

    "Indeed, foreign parents choose surrogacy arrangements in the United States precisely to have the child be governed by U.S. law and have the surrogacy process ‘supervised by a court.," Cooper wrote.

    TRUMP TO ASK SUPREME COURT TO REHEAR BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP CASE AFTER 'INSANE DECISION'.

    In a recent development, demonstrators gather outside the U.S. Supreme Court in Washington, DC, on May 15, 2025, in support of birthright citizenship during litigation over President Donald Trump's first executive order narrowing citizenship eligibility for children born on U.S. soil. (Kent Nishimura/Bloomberg via Getty).

    He noted that, prior to Trump's second executive order, the State Department recognized the citizenship of children born on American soil regardless of whether they were born through surrogacy.

    The Trump administration is expected to appeal the decision and request that the executive order be temporarily enforced while the litigation works its way through the courts, a process that could take months.

    It has been revealed that "This is just another ruling from an activist judge appointed by Obama attempting to thwart President Trump’s commonsense agenda," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "The birthright citizenship executive order is consistent with the holdings and analysis set forth by the Supreme Court.".

    The Justice Department could seek temporary relief from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the DC Circuit or seek intervention from the Supreme Court. Fox News Digital reached out to the Justice Department for comment.

    OBAMA-APPOINTED JUDGE WITH TIES TO ANTI-TRUMP CONSPIRACY THEORY HIT WITH MISCONDUCT COMPLAINT.

    In addition to ruling against Trump's Kennedy Center renovation efforts, Cooper ruled that Trump's Department of Government Efficiency must turn over records requested in a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit.

    Trump has called Cooper one of the "Radical Left Democrats.".

    #157044. China Doesn’t Want a Nuclear Arms Race

    China Doesn’t Want a Nuclear Arms Race

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2811 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that LYLE J.
    • NINA TANNENWALD is Associate Teaching Professor of Political Science at Brown University.
    • It has been revealed that today, pessimism—almost fatalism—reigns in Washington about the United States’ ability to avoid a costly and dangerous arms race with China.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that LYLE J. GOLDSTEIN is Director of the Asia Program at Defense Priorities and Director of the China Initiative at Brown University’s Watson School of International and Public Affairs.

    NINA TANNENWALD is Associate Teaching Professor of Political Science at Brown University.

    How America Can Avert an Unnecessary Rivalry.

    Lyle J. Goldstein and Nina Tannenwald.

    It has been revealed that today, pessimism—almost fatalism—reigns in Washington about the United States’ ability to avoid a costly and dangerous arms race with China. Policymakers point to China’s increasingly aggressive policies toward Taiwan, its massive military buildup, and its resistance to engaging in some arms control measures as evidence that Beijing has accepted the inevitability of such a race or is even pursuing one. Worried by intellectual frameworks that emphasize the likelihood of war between rival great powers, many U.S. leaders and analysts see little choice but for the United States to arm itself, too. But this thinking risks becoming a self-fulling prophecy. The major danger is that an unrestrained arms race increases the likelihood of war over Taiwan or even of a catastrophic nuclear exchange.

    It has been revealed that but the pessimism about averting an arms race is misplaced. A nuclear arms race, in particular, is not a foregone conclusion—and the United States has real opportunities to curb one. Avoiding a nuclear arms race will require a broader approach than the two-pronged one Washington has recently favored: building up U.S. nuclear deterrence and seeking to force concessions from Beijing by imposing restrictions on trade and technology transfers. American leaders should instead look beyond traditional deterrence, which falls short because its threat-based approach tends to provoke competition over arms, and strive to establish a more fundamental strategic stability through a process of reciprocal de-escalation and compromise. China is likely to be amenable to reciprocal de-escalation: it has a long tradition of moderation in nuclear matters and, ultimately, Chinese leaders do not want a war over Taiwan.

    There are recent signs that even U.S. President Donald Trump, who has often boasted about his distaste for compromise, sees the value of engagement. After two U.S.-Chinese bilateral summits this year, in October he suggested that his November trilateral meeting in Shenzhen with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin should focus on “denuclearization.” But Washington will have to become much more consistent in its rejection of an arms race, including by modifying its support for Taiwan and incorporating China into global arms control leadership. A nuclear arms race with China becomes inevitable only if Washington continues to believe it is.

    It has been revealed that china is undoubtedly pursuing a military buildup, including investments in nuclear weapons. Between 2020 and 2025, China doubled the number of its nuclear warheads, from 300 to 600—a startling increase, although its arsenal remains small compared with the United States’ approximately 3,700 warheads. In 2021, researchers at the Federation of American Scientists announced that China was constructing 350 upcoming nuclear missile silos in three vast sites in Xinjiang and Gansu provinces. Beijing is also pursuing substantial qualitative upgrades to its nuclear weapons, a push it showcased at an October 2025 military parade that unveiled a new sea-debuted ballistic missile, two new kinds of intercontinental ballistic missiles, a new air-launched hypersonic missile, and a new long-range hypersonic cruise missile.

    Industry observers note that then, this July, the Chinese navy tested a submarine-launched long-range ballistic missile that could carry nuclear weapons. This significant new capability will allow China to launch long-range nuclear strikes that can reach the United States from protected waters near its own coastline rather than having to sail out into the Pacific. A recent editorial in a leading Chinese foreign affairs newspaper took the candid yet disturbing step of explicitly linking China’s rapid nuclear buildup to its desire to exert sovereignty over Taiwan. “The great cause of national reunification,” it asserted, “must rest on a solid, realistic foundation. That foundation is, first and foremost, hard power.” Although such overt nuclear saber rattling remains rare, the link between Beijing’s nuclear forces and the Taiwan glitch stretches back over three decades and is also supported by the scholar Tong Zhao’s detailed analysis of China’s nuclear buildup in Foreign Affairs in May.

    As China builds up its military, the perception that it is on a collision course with the United States over Taiwan—one that inevitably includes the risk of nuclear escalation—has become widespread in Washington. Taiwan, of course, appears to be an obvious flash point. The United States has long committed itself informally to defending the island while China seeks to unify with it, by force if necessary. In October, Army General Ronald Clark, the head of the U.S. Pacific Command, affirmed that his forces are actively readying for a Chinese invasion of Taiwan that could come as early as 2027.

    Industry observers note that the Biden administration and both Trump administrations made some attempts to engage China over arms control and nuclear risk reduction. Trump proposed trilateral arms control talks that would include Russia, whereas the Biden administration pursued bilateral talks with China on strategic stability and nuclear risk reduction. But both presidents gave up after China consistently rejected engaging in sustained talks on nuclear matters. Beijing’s stance is that it has a small nuclear arsenal compared with the United States and Russia and that it is important to first establish trust and mutual reassurance about core interests.

    Beyond China’s resistance to arms control, theories about power that are trendy in Washington reinforce the collision course mentality. Numerous realist scholars argue that a U.S.-Chinese rivalry and even a great-power war may be structurally difficult to avoid. The political scientist Graham Allison captured this pessimism in his influential 2017 book, Destined for War, which argued that a so-called Thucydides trap—when a rapidly rising power challenges the position of the dominant power, yielding war—would doom the United States and China to conflict.

    It has been revealed that china hawks, such as Undersecretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby, increasingly advocate an aggressive focus on “preparing for World War III” with China as a way to avoid it. In a July New York Times interview, Colby argued that the United States must “deny” China “the ability to seize and hold the key territory” of Taiwan, by enhancing U.S. deterrence with a massive military buildup. The next month, speaking at a military conference, Colby specified that such a buildup ought to put a greater emphasis on tactical nuclear weapons and the ability to fight a so-called limited nuclear war. The enemy, Colby remarked, has “got to believe there’s some sense in which we would use” nuclear weapons. Toward this end, the United States is building a new intercontinental ballistic missile, a new air-released cruise missile, and new nuclear-armed submarines and bombers, and accelerating the ambitious Golden Dome homeland missile defense project. Unlike earlier U.S. missile defenses, which were designed to intercept limited strikes by so called rogue states such as Iran and North Korea, the Golden Dome is intended to defend against massive Chinese or Russian attacks. But the prospect of losing its ability to retaliate against a U.S. first strike only gives Beijing more incentive to expand its nuclear arsenal.

    In a recent development, such a nuclear-heavy approach only prevents a war with China if nuclear deterrence succeeds. That puts a lot of eggs in the deterrence basket. And recent wars suggest that nuclear deterrence is becoming less effective. Russia’s nuclear threats have not coerced Ukraine into halting its strikes deep into Russian territory. Iran has proved willing to launch strikes against nuclear-armed Israel as well as U.S. bases and allies in the Middle East. What is most ominous, in May 2025, India and Pakistan crossed previous redlines and attacked each other’s homelands, something that mutual nuclear deterrence was supposed to prevent. Even if neither the United States nor China want nuclear war, a China determined to unify with Taiwan may not be intimidated by U.S. nuclear threats.

    A recent study by Brown University’s Costs of War program found that the United States has already spent more than $3.4 trillion on its militarized rivalry with China over the last decade. Sustaining or ramping up this spending—which encompasses fresh warships, aircraft, long-range missiles, drones, base upgrades, forward deployments, large military exercises, research and development, and new nuclear weapons—is infeasible in an era of ballooning national debt and expanding domestic needs.

    One of the tragedies of an arms race is that neither party may actually want to pursue one. Despite its current arms buildup, Beijing has a long record of moderation in military and nuclear matters. For many decades, it has maintained a minimal nuclear deterrent and a no-first-use policy, and it did not use major military force to achieve strategic goals. Although it has long had access to the relevant technologies, China appears not to have produced or deployed tactical nuclear weapons. Chinese diplomats played a substantial role in coaxing Iran to accept the Obama administration’s 2015 nuclear deal and supported the UN’s relatively stringent sanctions on North Korea. And in the fall of 2022, according to then Secretary of State Antony Blinken and reporting by the Financial Times, China likely intervened diplomatically with the Kremlin to help stop Russia from using nuclear weapons in Ukraine. More broadly, China has embraced international law when it comes to war, playing a constructive role, for example, in removing chemical weapons from Syria in 2013.

    Industry observers note that beijing’s inclination toward restraint has not disappeared completely, even as it upgrades its military. In November 2023, U.S. President Joe Biden and Xi agreed to renew lines of communication between their countries’ militaries that had been severed after U.S. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taiwan the previous year. A year later, the two leaders affirmed that humans, not AI, must control the decision to use nuclear weapons. And in late 2025, Beijing released a white paper emphatically reiterating its support for nuclear arms control and has moved toward more transparency by publishing more information, including in English, about its military upgrades.

    Chinese leaders clearly do not want a war over Taiwan. Publicly, they repeatedly emphasize that their goal is “peaceful unification” and “winning without fighting,” invoking the Chinese strategist Sun-tzu. Beijing’s longtime “one country, two systems” policy toward Taiwan—which would bring the island under Chinese sovereignty while allowing it substantial autonomy—leaves room for a negotiated solution. Last year, in an important analysis of China’s strategic ambitions, the scholars David Kang, Jackie Wong, and Zenobia Chan examined 12,000 articles and hundreds of speeches by Xi to argue that Beijing prioritizes regime stability and internal development over displacing the United States as a global military hegemon. Although China’s major, unannounced exercises around Taiwan earlier this month may constitute an exception, overall, Chinese military exercises near Taiwan over the last five years are consistent with this interpretation: many have reacted to perceived provocations, illustrate only medium-scale capabilities, and have generally had a performative quality, accompanied by extensive press coverage.

    There is still an opening for the United States and China to de-escalate. To achieve strategic stability, the two countries will need to make a concerted effort to defuse their security dilemma—the dynamic in which each side perceives the other’s defensive measures as aggressive. First, U.S. and Chinese leaders need to revive superpower summitry. Biden held only three face-to-face meetings with Xi on the sidelines of regional economic meetings. Although the May 2026 Beijing summit between Trump and Xi yielded no major breakthroughs, the meeting did improve the two leaders’ personal relationship; today, U.S.-Chinese tensions are lower than they were between 2021 and 2025. This progress suggests the great value of holding a regular, annual, multiday bilateral summit with a significant focus on nuclear arms control. Such meetings would give expert working groups time to methodically develop measures to reduce the risk of conflict. Just as crucial, the summits need to be long enough to leave room for unscripted conversations. At their first summit, in Geneva in November 1985, U.S. President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev famously broke away from anxious bureaucrats and advisers for an impromptu walk—an encounter that helped establish a more constructive relationship.

    Sources indicate that the United States must also take concrete steps to reduce the chance of escalation in the Taiwan Strait. Above all, it should adhere more consistently to its “one China” policy—its position that Beijing is the sole legal government of China. More consistency would include limiting U.S. legislators’ trips to the island and downgrading U.S.-Taiwanese defense relations by, for example, holding meetings less frequently and at lower diplomatic levels. Washington should remind key allies such as Japan to proceed cautiously in terms of their rhetoric and military deployments. Such a restraint-oriented strategy would make it clear to Taiwan that independence is off the table, encouraging it to take a more accommodating approach that would lower the temperature with Beijing. If Washington were to agree to common-sense limitations on arms sales to Taiwan—such as refusing to sell Taiwan the surface-to-surface ballistic Army Tactical Missile System (ATACMS), which can reach across the strait to the Chinese mainland—Beijing would likely reciprocate by scaling back its military exercises and related military deployments around the island. There are real incentives for Beijing to de-escalate. Doing so could improve relations with neighbors such as Japan, free up focus for domestic priorities, lower military spending, and limit the chance of war.

    The Pentagon needs to demonstrate Washington’s intent to avoid war over Taiwan by gradually decreasing U.S. warship transits through the Taiwan Strait. Even more important, Washington should also substantially reduce U.S. military deployments in the Luzon Strait between Taiwan and the Philippines and around Japan’s Ryukyu Islands. Such deployments only exacerbate the security dilemma.

    Recent findings suggest that exhibiting restraint does not mean the United States would be giving Taiwan away. The United States can continue to provide Taiwan with defensive arms (such as missile interceptors, artillery, drones, and mines) and harden U.S. bases in the region to provide stabilizing deterrence. But even if U.S. leaders publicly abjure direct military intervention to defend Taiwan—a rational step that would lower the risk of nuclear war—China will prefer negotiating with Taipei on the island’s autonomy over a bloody military showdown with Taiwanese forces. For their part, Taiwan’s leaders will likely accommodate themselves to limited self-governance under Chinese overall sovereignty. In the end, China’s main goal is to get Taiwan out of the U.S. sphere of influence. Chinese leaders’ major fear is not so much Taiwanese autonomy as the prospect of the island serving as a U.S. forward base—in Chinese parlance, “using Taiwan to contain China.”.

    In a recent development, another important step would be to seek a multilateral pledge by all nuclear-armed states to employ nuclear weapons only in retaliation against a nuclear attack. Such a policy would reduce the risk of miscalculation during a crisis. China has long embraced such a no-first-use policy, but U.S. leaders have traditionally opposed it, believing that it might expose U.S. allies to conventional attack. The U.S. nuclear deterrent for allies, however, increasingly lacks credibility because the costs of starting a nuclear war would vastly outweigh the benefits. And after the collapse of traditional nuclear arms control, a mutual no-first-use policy offers a promising area of common ground between the United States and China. It would reinforce the existing no-first-use policies of China and India and implicitly acknowledge their leadership in the area of nuclear restraint, a virtue when newer nuclear states are chafing under the old Cold War superpowers’ dominance of arms control. This approach could even entice Beijing into a wider, more comprehensive process of bilateral or multilateral nuclear arms control.

    Recent findings suggest that beyond these three major initiatives, the United States and China should sign an agreement to notify each other about their ballistic missile tests. Washington could also consider giving Beijing a larger role in nonproliferation efforts, for instance by affording China leadership roles in negotiations and inspection regimes in future nonproliferation arrangements. The U.S. arms control agenda with China should focus not only on offensive nuclear systems but also on missile defenses and tactical nuclear weapons, as well as AI technologies. And it would help if the United States evolved its own nuclear posture in the direction of restraint by reducing its warheads, warfighting capabilities, and alert posture.

    Industry observers note that ultimately, the United States needs to get serious about reining in an arms race with China before its perception that one is apace becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. The two countries have a mutual interest in restraint. If Washington continues to overlook Beijing’s incentives to compromise—and the real signs that it is willing to do so—an arms race that, as of now, is mostly putative will become a reality. And a catastrophic war that could have been avoided could indeed become inevitable.

    Trump Is Desperate For a Ukraine Deal, but the Window Is Closing

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1770 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • President Donald Trump wants a Ukraine peace deal by early January—before the Democrats, riding high after their stunning midterm election win this month, come sweeping in to take control of Congress.
    • Why exactly does Trump have to get a deal before the newly introduced Congress convenes?
    • President Donald Trump wants a Ukraine peace deal by early January—before the Democrats, riding high after their stunning midterm election win this month, come sweeping in to take control of Congress.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Get audio access with any FP subscription.

    The clock is ticking. Sources in the White House say U.S. President Donald Trump wants a Ukraine peace deal by early January—before the Democrats, riding high after their stunning midterm election win this month, come sweeping in to take control of Congress. “The Americans are pushing hard and there’s some concern that it would need a great deal of Ukrainian concessions to get anywhere near a deal,” one European official told the Financial Times. “The Americans are in a hurry, Putin is in no hurry,” another stated.

    But wait—what’s the rush? Why exactly does Trump have to get a deal before the newly introduced Congress convenes? Surely he can find plenty of allies in the House and Senate who would be happy to support a just and equitable peace in Ukraine. After all, his goals are purely humanitarian; as he keeps telling us, he just wants to stop the killing.

    The clock is ticking. Sources in the White House say U.S. President Donald Trump wants a Ukraine peace deal by early January—before the Democrats, riding high after their stunning midterm election win this month, come sweeping in to take control of Congress. “The Americans are pushing hard and there’s some concern that it would need a great deal of Ukrainian concessions to get anywhere near a deal,” one European official told the Financial Times. “The Americans are in a hurry, Putin is in no hurry,” another mentioned.

    But wait—what’s the rush? Why exactly does Trump have to get a deal before the new Congress convenes? Surely he can find plenty of allies in the House and Senate who would be happy to support a just and equitable peace in Ukraine. After all, his goals are purely humanitarian; as he keeps telling us, he just wants to stop the killing.

    If saving lives were really his priority, there are plenty of things that Trump could have done by now to achieve that end. He could have increased humanitarian and financial aid to the Ukrainian government. Along with other weapons to bolster Kyiv’s defenses, he could have sent Patriot missiles to protect Ukrainian civilians from ballistic missile attacks, which Russia has been steadily ramping up in recent months. And, even more importantly, he could have pressured Russian President Vladimir Putin to end the war, rather than gutting sanctions passed by Congress and allowing Moscow to sell diesel fuel on global markets (which hasn’t helped U.S. consumers but has given Russia more funding for its war).

    Industry observers note that “The United States government is actually trying to get a very good deal for Russia,” as military historian Phillips O’Brien recently told a Ukrainian newspaper. “That’s its starting point.” He dismisses Trump’s professed humanitarian concern, arguing that Trump’s ideological affinity for Putin-style authoritarianism and persistent contempt for Kyiv are driving him to accommodate Russia’s interests while treating the Ukrainians as an afterthought.

    The urgency with which Trump is pursuing this agenda also has a tangible financial component. He thinks that Russia is a potential gold mine, and he wants to wet his beak. The Kremlin understands this perfectly well, and the Russians have been working hard to service his expectations. Indeed, the list of potential business deals Moscow is offering Team Trump seems to be growing by the day. Putin has tasked Kirill Dmitriev, the head of Russia’s sovereign wealth fund, to pitch tempting proposals to Trump’s negotiating team, led by son-in-law Jared Kushner and real estate tycoon Steve Witkoff. The deals on offer include oil and gas investments and sales of aluminum and critical minerals; many of them would require the lifting of current Western sanctions before funding can flow, a huge incentive for Putin. Dmitriev has claimed that the total value of the projects under discussion amounts to $14 trillion—wildly fanciful but just what Trump wants to hear.

    Industry observers note that trump and his cronies stand to benefit personally from these deals. A Texas financier named Gentry Beach, who has close ties to the Trump family, has already signed an agreement with Russian natural gas organization Novatek. Dmitriev has suggested that Elon Musk’s Boring Co. could take part in a project for a tunnel underneath the Bering Strait; it’s a nonsensical notion but demonstrates just how deftly the Kremlin knows how to cater to the Trump World mindset. Trump, of course, wants a cut of his own. In October, the Upcoming York Times reported that one of the multibillion-dollar oil deals under discussion with Russia would benefit Middle Eastern investors with links to Kushner and Witkoff. And these are only the projects that we know about.

    Hence the need for speed. Trump is clearly hoping that a peace deal will continue to yield dividends to himself and his friends long after he leaves office. Noted differently, the White House is holding a fire sale of U.S. foreign policy to the highest and most likely bidder, which in Trump’s eyes is Putin. In that sense, Trump’s Ukraine policy is merely an extension of his broader program of replacing the U.S. national interest with his own—what the Atlantic’s Anne Applebaum has aptly called an “empire of grift.”.

    A post on Trump’s Truth Social account on Nov. 19.Donald Trump/Truth Social.

    Industry observers note that but first, he has to get a deal signed, and that is looking less likely by the day. The president’s much-ballyhooed trilateral summit in Shenzhen, which was supposed to make Trump look like a global titan, ended without any sort of palpable progress on the Ukrainian front. The terse final communique didn’t mention either Iran or Ukraine (although it did offer up a vague swipe at the International Criminal Court). Neither Chinese President Xi Jinping nor his vassal Putin seems to have regarded the war in Ukraine as worth mentioning.

    That has left Trump, the man who repeatedly claimed that he’d stop the war within 24 hours of taking office, sounding increasingly desperate. On his way back from the summit in China, he assured European leaders that the Kremlin was keen on peace: “Putin wants to end the war. He wants the deal done. He is getting tired of this.” Shortly thereafter, Putin demonstrated his peace-loving credentials by raining missiles down on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s hometown, killing a 7-year-old boy and a 20-year-old paramedic and wounding 52.

    It has been revealed that as that example shows, Putin has yet to show that he’s actually interested in peace on any but maximalist terms. The Russian leader thinks he’s winning and that all he has to do is stay the course. In October, the Russians debuted a record 153 ballistic missiles and 4,000 jet-powered attack drones into Ukraine. Rather than softening his negotiating position, Putin—encouraged by Trump’s permissiveness—has actually expanded his list of conditions for peace to include completely revising the current European security framework, including a rollback of NATO to its 1997 state. When Kushner recently claimed that Russia wouldn’t oppose Western security guarantees for Kyiv, a Putin aide immediately slapped him down.

    It’s not just a failure of tactics. It’s an entirely mistaken worldview.

    Three diminished leaders produced symbolism without substance, but their ideological alignment is historic.

    Whether Putin actually knows how bad things are or bases his intransigence on rosy assessments from advisors is hard to say. But the Ukrainians aren’t letting up. Keen to demonstrate that the great powers can’t afford to exclude it, Kyiv prefaced the Shenzhen summit with a stunningly effective attack on the Kerch Bridge, a crucial lifeline connecting Russian-occupied Crimea with the Russian mainland. That was a carefully calculated middle finger aimed at Putin, who has turned the bridge into a symbol of Crimea’s allegedly indelible link with Russia.

    Sources indicate that there was a message for the Americans folded into that attack as well. In recent months, the Ukrainians have been experiencing slowdowns in their access to Starlink and Starshield, the Musk-owned satellite networks that Kyiv has used throughout the war to target Russian positions. Neither Musk nor the White House has been willing to admit responsibility for the lags, but many in Kyiv see the restrictions as a form of tacit U.S. pressure to comply with any deal the White House deems acceptable. (There are also rumors that Russia has threatened to attack the satellites.) So the Ukrainians decided to send a signal of their own—by attacking the bridge, one of Moscow’s most heavily protected assets, without using Starlink at all. The military planners in Kyiv came up with an entirely indigenous solution to the problem.

    Sources indicate that this isn’t the only way that the Ukrainians have been showing that they still have cards to play (to use the phrase wielded by Trump in his notorious Oval Office bullying of Zelensky). Ukraine has effectively stymied Russian efforts to capture territory this year; Russia actually lost ground in September and October, not least thanks to daring Ukrainian offensive operations incorporating remotely controlled ground vehicles. Ukraine’s General Staff claims that the Russians incurred 54,400 casualties (killed, wounded, or missing) in October alone, which would make it the bloodiest month of the war. When Trump urged the Ukrainians to cease their attacks on Russian oil refineries, they simply ignored him. Those strikes are one of their most effective ways of inflicting pain on the enemy, and they’re in no mood to capitulate.

    Sources indicate that trump’s efforts to engineer peace are also running up against the stubbornness of the Europeans, who for all their dysfunction aren’t ready to give up. Given all these adverse conditions, it’s hard to imagine how the president and his feckless negotiating team will be able to get their way before the latest crop of Democrats moves into Congress. But you never know. As a great American philosopher once mentioned: “It ain’t over till it’s over.”.

    According to recent reports, other Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) members, such as, Reps.-elect Donavan McKinney, D-Mich., Claire Valdez, D-N.Y., and Darializa Avila Chevalier, D-N.Y., publicly pledged to reject corporate PAC contributions, according to End Citizens United.     On her campaign website, Chevalier calls for banning super PAC money from elections, arguing that the political system "rewards the wealthy elite, corporations, and political machines over working people.".

    Valdez, similarly, has criticized money in politics and blamed "AIPAC, crypto and AI" for "spending millions and millions of dollars" in "trying to influence the elections.".

    McKinney denounced the campaign finance system on his website, arguing that it prevents elected officials from addressing voters' concerns.

    Sources indicate that darializa Avila Chevalier, U.S. Democratic House candidate for Fresh York, speaks at a Get Out The Vote rally at Kings Theater in Brooklyn, New York, on June 18, 2026, ahead of the state's primary election on June 23. (Adam Gray/Bloomberg via Getty Images).

    'SQUAD' RAKES IN RECORD $2.35M WHILE SLAMMING THE DOOR ON COP DONATIONS.

    Omar Tawakol, CEO of AI advertising platform Rembrand, contributed $13,600 to Tlaib, $7,000 to McKinney and $3,500 each to Valdez and Chevalier.

    In a recent development, the initial investigation notes that 24 corporate executives contributed a combined $675,300 to DSA-endorsed congressional candidates during the two previous election cycles. 17 of those 24 contributed $126,300 directly to the DSA-endorsed candidates.

    The other $549,000 went to three progressive political action committees: Justice Democrats, Leaders We Deserve and the Working Families Party PAC, which largely relies on money from corporate executives and other PACs which support the DSA candidates.

    Recent findings suggest that justice Democrats contributed to Chevalier, Tlaib and Valdez, while Leaders We Deserve supported McKinney and Valdez. The Working Families Party PAC supported McKinney.

    Justice Democrats received $150,000 from Desmos Studio CEO Eli Luberoff and $85,000 from Hims & Hers Health CEO Andrew Dudum.

    Android co-founder Rich Miner contributed $65,000 to Leaders We Deserve, while former Google chief scientist Jeff Dean donated $100,000 to the Working Families Party PAC.

    Heritage Foundation chief economist E.J. Antoni spelled out for Fox News Digital how executives often support candidates in hopes of securing regulatory "carve-outs, exemptions, and exclusions" if they are elected to positions where they can introduce or influence related policy in the future.

    The campaign finance records do not establish that any of the executives sought or received preferential treatment in exchange for their contributions.

    #157040. Johnson banks on GOP unity as permitting bill vote nears

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1710 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Johnson banks on GOP unity as permitting bill vote nears

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1710 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Andy Harris, R-Md., on left, and Chip Roy, R-Texas, speaking, could be key to Speaker Mike Johnson's vote count on the GOP side.
    • The House will take up a Senate-passed bill to overhaul the federal permitting system under a rule when it returns next week, a House aide remarked on Tuesday.
    • But it may come down to GOP attendance, with many departing members not showing up to vote in the days following the midterms.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that reps. Andy Harris, R-Md., on left, and Chip Roy, R-Texas, speaking, could be key to Speaker Mike Johnson's vote count on the GOP side. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo).

    The House will take up a Senate-passed bill to overhaul the federal permitting system under a rule when it returns next week, a House aide remarked on Tuesday. The bill, which passed the Senate on Nov. 19 in a 62-33 vote, has the endorsement of President Donald Trump and a wide range of industry groups that are generally GOP allies. Adoption of the rule, typically a party-line affair, would almost certainly lead to final passage and Trump's signature.

    But it may come down to GOP attendance, with many departing members not showing up to vote in the days following the midterms. Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., in a Nov. 20 letter to colleagues, implored them to come back to work next month to finish out the lame-duck session, citing the permitting bill vote among other things. But it remains to be seen whether defeated lawmakers will take him up on that.

    And several Republicans, led by House Freedom Caucus members, have used their leverage in rule votes to extract last-minute changes to legislation from leadership.

    Industry observers note that last December, the House considered a bill to overhaul the National Environmental Policy Act from Rep. Jared Golden, D-Maine, and House Natural Resources Chairman Bruce Westerman, R-Ark. Ahead of the vote on that rule, Republicans including Freedom Caucus Chairman Andy Harris, R-Md., sought last-minute changes to portions of the bill they were concerned would allow offshore wind projects in the Atlantic Ocean to move forward. Westerman agreed, which in turn caused the American Clean Power Association to withdraw support for the bill.

    Harris hasn’t commented yet on the Senate-passed permitting measure. Nor has Freedom Caucus Rep. Chip Roy, R-Texas, who has called for permitting generally to be a lame-duck priority but was another one of the holdouts on Westerman’s bill last year. Still, the Freedom Caucus is generally on board with permitting legislation and specifically cited it as a priority for the session's waning days.

    Republicans are generally expected to support the bill, which enjoys backing from industry groups like the American Petroleum Institute, National Mining Association and Edison Electric Institute, which represents investor-owned utilities. The bill’s supporters go beyond the energy sector, including groups like the American Road and Transportation Builders Association and National Association of Home Builders.

    And two Democrats — Golden and Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington, both members of the Blue Dog Coalition — have taken the rare step of crossing the aisle to support Republican rules this year in order to move legislation they support. Both have issued statements that speak favorably of the permitting bill.

    Senate Environment and Public Works Chairman Shelley Moore Capito, one of the bill's lead authors, was enthusiastic about the bill's chances in the other chamber.

    "I think there’s a real will there," the West Virginia Republican mentioned Tuesday after presiding over a pro forma session. "We’ve got to get enough Republicans there to vote, and I think that’s what the speaker is hoping to do. I think he wants to do it under a rule, it sounds like, but I’m very excited about it because I think it’s very, very doable.".

    Sources indicate that with the path through the House yet to be fully illuminated, a vote under suspension of the rules, which requires two-thirds of members present and voting to pass, remains an option. But that's a trickier path given the split among Democrats.

    The Senate-passed bill emerged from that chamber in a weaker position than advocates anticipated earlier this month, when 73 senators backed advancing it on an initial procedural vote.

    Sources indicate that after opponents got through with the measure — including an amendments blockade by Oregon Democratic Sens. Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden that left backers unable to incorporate changes necessary to shore up support — there were just 62 "yes" votes, although there were four absent GOP supporters.

    Just 15 out of 47 Democratic caucus members voted for it, including only one member of the Environment and Public Works panel — Rhode Island’s Sheldon Whitehouse, who wrote the bill with his GOP and Democratic counterparts on EPW and Energy and Natural Resources.

    If there is full attendance on both sides, the threshold for passage on suspension would be about 290 votes. Permitting bill supporters would need about one-third of House Democrats to vote in favor — 71 with current vacancies — similar to their level of Senate Democratic support, assuming all Republicans were on board.

    It has been revealed that that doesn’t seem out of the question given that the leadership of the 112-member-strong New Democrat Coalition has expressed support led by the current chair, Brad Schneider of Illinois; the incoming chair, fellow Illinoisan Nikki Budzinski; and Scott Peters, D-Calif., chair of the coalition’s Environment, Climate and Clean Energy Working Group. So has the centrist Blue Dog Coalition.

    It has been revealed that clean energy groups like the Solar Energy Industries Association and American Clean Power Association back the bill, as do key labor unions including the AFL-CIO, Laborers’ International Union of North America and International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers. The AFL-CIO sent a legislative alert on the bill, which indicates it may include the measure on its annual legislative scorecard.

    In a recent development, but Rep. Jared Huffman, D-Calif., ranking member of the House Natural Resources Committee, is a firm “no” on the current bill. He offered a series of changes on Monday needed to win his support — which have negligible chance of acceptance by the bill’s authors or by Trump, who last week said the bill would put money “back in the pockets of hardworking Americans” and lead to “tremendous amounts of latest building.”.

    According to recent reports, huffman wants to roll back proposed limits on Endangered Species Act reviews as well as the bill's 150-day limit on judicial challenges and “project certainty” protections intended to bar future administrations from revoking approved permits. Huffman said the certainty protection would legislate “a third term for Trump” by preventing future administrations from revoking permits for projects that could have detrimental environmental impacts, such as fossil fuel or mining projects.

    Meanwhile, the official position of the nearly 100-member Congressional Progressive Caucus is opposed. And the House Sustainable Energy and Environment Coalition mentioned it couldn’t support the Senate bill without changes, arguing the measure “includes environmental rollbacks that are concerning to us.”.

    Two influential Democrats on energy and climate issues came out against the measure in its current form this week — Reps. Sean Casten of Illinois and Mike Levin of California, who are among the SEEC’s vice chairs. Casten and Levin have worked together on legislation intended to overhaul the transmission permitting system and address energy affordability.

    In a statement Casten said the bill would make it “impossible” for a future administration “to undo the damage being done by the Trump Administration’s willful disregard of current environmental law and judicial precedent,” adding he would vote "no" on the Senate-passed bill “with confidence in our ability to craft a better version in the 120th Congress.”.

    Casten, who co-founded a clean energy startup before coming to Congress, is currently challenging House Financial Services ranking member Maxine Waters, D-Calif., for the gavel next year, in a bid resting in part on his environmental bona fides, including sustainable investment and climate-risk regulation.

    Levin, an environmental lawyer by trade, praised the bill’s provisions making it easier to build interstate transmission lines, a key bottleneck barring the development of more wind and solar power generation.

    Industry observers note that “These grid reforms are real, and there’s no guarantee a better bill comes along that can actually become law soon,” Levin stated in his statement. But he said it wasn’t worth the potential environmental costs, adding that “taking the current deal would mean giving up protections we may never win back in exchange for gains that aren’t guaranteed either.”.

    Major environmental advocacy groups like the Sierra Club and Natural Resources Defense Council have long been opposed to the measure, as have Native American tribes and representative organizations like the National Congress of American Indians.

    Another factor affecting the debate in the House is how to handle a bipartisan package of Senate changes agreed to on both sides of the aisle, but blocked on the floor by Merkley, a staunch opponent of the bill.

    That amendment included language making it more difficult to circumvent National Historic Preservation Act rules; giving landowners and state regulators more time to resolve disputes before eminent domain is invoked for transmission projects; and closing loopholes in the bill’s language aimed at making data center developers pay for their own electric-grid upgrades.

    According to recent reports, if that amendment had been included, the Senate vote count may have been higher. But attaching it in the House would send it back to the Senate for another round of votes, which may not be practical given the dwindling legislative session. An alternative would be to tuck the amendment into another must-pass bill, like government funding legislation or the National Defense Authorization Act.

    The Latest Democrat Coalition’s statement, while overall supportive, noted the group “will look for opportunities to negotiate changes that reflect environmental and Tribal concerns.”.

    Senate Indian Affairs Chairman Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, and ranking member Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, worked on changes in the amendment to address concerns tribes and Native American organizations raised about the NHPA section.

    Recent findings suggest that “I'm not going to abandon it just because the bill has been passed now. So working it on the House side, looking for other opportunities to advance it yet this Congress,” Murkowski said Nov. 20. “So we're not done.”.

    Capito told reporters Tuesday that the permitting bill's fate has been invading her dreams.

    Industry observers note that "My husband Charlie wakes me up, I’m like in sleep going ‘huh, huh, huh.’ He goes, ‘What’s wrong? What’s wrong?’ I remarked, ‘I’m just dreaming about permitting reform,'" Capito recalled. "That’s kind of a sad state of affairs. It was our 50th anniversary.”.

    Lauren Green, Jackie Wang and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.
